From the perspective of a computer science researcher, let me give my answer based on what we teach in an AI class (AI: A Modern Approach).

There are four viewpoints for AI:

  • A computer which think like humans
  • A computer which think rationally
  • A computer which acts like humans
  • A computer which acts rationally

Thinking and consciousness are topics worth discussion. Because there is no concrete definition of thinking, most AI research has been conducted with systems that simply act. There is something called the Chinese room argument, which states that if a computer were to act like it was thinking convincingly enough it would be sufficiently thinking for anyone interacting with it.

HOWEVER, it is possible that at some point in the future we will nail down thinking/consciousness and grant the ability of an AI system to do the same. It just seems a distant goal for right now.

The problem is that powerful industries build up around these large scale programs (I.E, corn ethanol). Therefor even when a program proves to be an all out farce it is nearly impossible to end no matter how wasteful and unsustainable the program.
I would like to discuss what I see as a downside to large scale federal and state "sustainability/green" (corn ethanol) programs.

Also as I am seeing more and more GIANT wind turbines lord over my neck of the woods I really wonder if the EXTREMELY substantial resources that go into the production and erection of wind turbines will ever be recouped. Also does the the increased demand for natural resources like copper encourage environmentally harmful developments such as The Pebble Mine?

The energy required to produce something (embodied energy) can be determined using Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), and I'd guess that there are some published data on wind turbines somewhere.

I researched the same question for solar panels, and the total energy output exceeded the embodied energy after only a couple years, so after 20+ years the system will have recouped the embodied energy many times over.

Thank you for your response. The Life Cycle Assessment on large wind turbines it would seem is estimated at worst to be about 1 year out of 20. This by it self seems like a pretty good number. There are other considerations that need to be taken into account when considering sustainability. For example, my family has a investment in a private gravel mine and over the last 10 or so years we have provided a lot of material to wind farm projects. As have other gravel pits in the vicinity. It is conceivable that the continued expansion of wind farms will in fact deplete the local gravel reserves. Also because of the need for generator redundancy do to the intermittent nature of wind generation wind energy creates a significant demand for materials like copper. The mining of copper has a substantial environmental impact outside of its contribution to embodied energy of a wind farm.

Edit: I guess that when ever it seems that a program is taking the "damn the torpedos full speed ahead" approach I get awfully nervous. I would be a lot more comfortable if we had an efficient means of storing the energy produced by these wind farms.

Much like any subsidy program, it inherently breeds dependence. I'm not against the government running programs like this, but we need to be smarter about how these are rolled out to make them easier to roll back if and when they are concluded.
I guess I am looking for suggestions as to how we become "smarter" in the way we implement these programs. I have put a fare amount of thought into this and have no idea how.

A key would be clearer funding. Instead of creating a guessing game by the program participants - where, for example, an inherently 6 year program, say solar equipment rebates, is only authorized for two years at a time indefinately (ultimately leading to a crash when it is unpredictably not extended).

This is no silver bullet, maybe only a shard of silver buckshot, but it would help.
